orthodox_qgd.name: Orthodox Defense

orthodox_qgd.black_plan: Solid with Be7-O-O-Nbd7-c6, aim for dxc4 and Nd5 exchanges, break with c5 or e5

after_Bg5.key_decision: The Bg5 pin is the hallmark of the Orthodox QGD

Be7.why_good: Classical and reliable - prepares to castle

h6.why_good: Forces Bh4, and Black can play g5 later

lasker_defense.name: Lasker Defense

lasker_defense.black_plan: Exchange pieces to ease the cramp, reach a playable endgame, break with e5

after_h6.key_decision: The Lasker Defense - Black plans Ne4 to simplify

Bh4.why_good: Standard - after Ne4 Bxe7 Qxe7, the position simplifies

Bxf6.why_good: Simpler - gives up bishop pair but avoids simplification

common_learnings: The QGD is one of the most classical and tested openings in chess

c5 and e5 are the two key breaks for Black in the middlegame
White's minority attack (b4-b5) is the main strategic plan
The Lasker Defense (h6/Ne4) is a great simplification tool for Black

traps.name: Marshall Trap
traps.explanation: White takes the d5 pawn and thinks they win the queen with Bxd8. But Bb4+ is an in-between check that forces Qd2, and Bxd2+ wins White's queen.
traps.refutation: Do NOT play Nxd5. The pawn is not free. Play e3 or Nf3.

traps.name: Elephant Trap
traps.explanation: After b5 and a6, Black plays Nxe4. If Bxe7 Qxe7 and then Bxe4, Bb7 hits the bishop on the long diagonal. White loses material.
traps.refutation: After b5, do not retreat bishop to d3. Play Be2 or a4.

modern_benoni.black_plan: Fianchetto Bg7, play on the kingside with f5 or center with e5, use the dark squares

after_d6.key_decision: The Modern Benoni structure is set - asymmetric and sharp

e4.why_good: White has a strong center with d5+e4

czech_benoni.name: Czech Benoni
czech_benoni.white_plan: Build a big center (e4+d5), slowly expand, use space advantage
czech_benoni.black_plan: Lock the center with e5, maneuver pieces to the kingside, break with f5 when ready

after_e5.key_decision: The Czech Benoni - a closed, strategic battle

Nc3.why_good: Build behind the pawn chain, prepare f4

common_learnings: The Benoni creates an asymmetric pawn structure - White has space, Black has dynamics
In the Modern Benoni, the d5 pawn is both White's strength and a target
Black's dark-square bishop on g7 is crucial - don't trade it
f5 is the key break for Black in most Benoni structures
The Czech Benoni (e5) leads to a slower, more maneuvering game

budapest_main.black_plan: Pressure e5 with Ng4 and Nc6, develop Bb4+ for tempo, recover the pawn

after_Ng4.key_decision: Black immediately targets the e5 pawn

Bf4.why_good: The most reliable - holds the pawn and develops

e4.idea: Bold - give up e5 for a big center
e4.why_good: After Nxe5, White has a strong center

fajarowicz_gambit.name: Fajarowicz Gambit (Ne4)
fajarowicz_gambit.white_plan: Don't panic - develop normally with Nf3-e3, keep the extra pawn
fajarowicz_gambit.black_plan: Ne4 is more ambitious than Ng4 - aim for piece activity and tactical tricks

Nf3.why_good: Don't overthink - develop and hold the pawn

Qd5.consequence: Black gets rapid development with tempo against the queen
Qd5.learning: Don't bring the queen out early to protect pawns - develop pieces instead

common_learnings: The Budapest is a surprise weapon - great for catching White off guard
Black sacrifices the e5 pawn for piece activity and development
Ng4 is the main move (more sound), Ne4 is the Fajarowicz (trickier)
White should stay calm, develop naturally, and hold the extra pawn
If White plays accurately, they keep a small edge - but practical chances are good for Black

traps.name: Kieninger Trap
traps.explanation: Smothered checkmate! Black's knight lands on d3 with check and White's own pieces block all escape. One of the most beautiful traps in chess.
traps.refutation: White should avoid the mechanical capture sequence. Be aware of the Nd3 mating square.

traps.name: Budapest Smothered Mate
traps.explanation: Smothered checkmate! White thinks axb4 wins a bishop but Nd3# is mate. The king is trapped by its own pieces.
traps.refutation: Play e3 or Nf3 on move 4, not Bf4. Do not allow the Bb4+ Qe7 sequence.

dutch_defense.name: Dutch Defense
dutch_defense.white_plan: Control the center, develop naturally, exploit the weakened kingside (e1-h5 diagonal)
dutch_defense.black_plan: Control e4 with f5, choose between Stonewall (d5), Leningrad (g6), or Classical (e6+Be7)

after_f5.key_decision: Black plays aggressively with f5 - controlling e4 is the priority

g3.why_good: Bg2 will pressure the center and fight for e4

c4.why_good: Flexible - can transpose to many systems

stonewall_dutch.name: Stonewall Dutch
stonewall_dutch.white_plan: Fianchetto Bg2, exploit the weak e5 square, play around the stonewall
stonewall_dutch.black_plan: Build the wall: d5+f5+e6+c6, develop Bd6 and aim for a kingside attack

Nf3.why_good: The Ne5 outpost is White's dream square in the Stonewall

cxd5.why_bad: Opens the position for Black's bishops
cxd5.consequence: After exd5 or cxd5, Black's pieces become very active
cxd5.learning: Don't exchange in the center against the Stonewall - play around it

leningrad_dutch.name: Leningrad Dutch
leningrad_dutch.white_plan: Develop with g3-Bg2-Nf3, challenge the center, exploit the weakened light squares
leningrad_dutch.black_plan: Fianchetto BOTH bishops (Bg7 + f5), play for e5 break, kingside attack

after_Bg7.key_decision: The Leningrad setup - double fianchetto with f5

Nf3.why_good: Prepares to castle and fight for the center

common_learnings: The Dutch is aggressive for Black - f5 controls e4 and aims for kingside play
The Stonewall (d5+f5) creates a fortress but leaves e5 weak
The Leningrad (g6+Bg7+f5) is more dynamic with the double fianchetto
The weak e1-h5 diagonal is Black's main vulnerability after f5
Black should always castle kingside quickly to protect the weakened king position

scandinavian_defense.name: Scandinavian Defense
scandinavian_defense.white_plan: Capture on d5, develop with tempo against the Black queen, build a central advantage
scandinavian_defense.black_plan: Challenge e4 immediately, develop the queen early or recapture with Nf6, solid but slightly behind

exd5.idea: Take the pawn - the only principled response
exd5.why_good: Forces Black to make a concession

scand_qxd5.name: Main Line (Qxd5)
scand_qxd5.white_plan: Develop with tempo (Nc3 gains time), build a strong center, pressure Black's queen
scand_qxd5.black_plan: Develop Qa5 (safe square), Nf6, Bf5 early (before e6!), castle and equalize

Qa5.idea: Safe and active - the modern main line
Qa5.why_good: Avoids further tempo loss, connects with Bd7/Bf5 plans

Qd6.why_good: Flexible - can support c5 or e5 breaks

Qe5+.why_bad: The queen will be kicked around
Qe5+.consequence: After Be2, Black has no good square for the queen
Qe5+.learning: Don't check just because you can - the queen needs a stable square

scand_nf6.name: Modern Scandinavian (Nf6)
scand_nf6.white_plan: Build a big center with d4+c4, develop naturally, use the space advantage
scand_nf6.black_plan: Recapture with Nf6-Nxd5, fianchetto Bg7, play for counterattack with c5 or e5

after_Nf6.key_decision: The Modern Scandinavian avoids early queen moves

d4.why_good: Natural - prepares c4 for a strong pawn duo

common_learnings: The Scandinavian immediately challenges e4 - direct and honest
After Qxd5 Nc3, the queen MUST move - losing a tempo is the cost
Qa5 is the modern main line - safe and active
The Nf6 variation avoids queen moves but gives White a bigger center
Bf5 should come out BEFORE e6 (same idea as the Caro-Kann and Slav)

traps.name: Scandinavian Queen Danger
traps.explanation: Nd5 attacks the queen and threatens Nxf6+ discovering an attack. Black's queen is overworked and must give up material.
traps.refutation: Black should castle quickly and not leave the queen exposed on a5 for too long.

nimzowitsch_defense.name: Nimzowitsch Defense

nimzowitsch_defense.black_plan: Hypermodern approach - let White build the center, then attack it with d5, f5, or e5

after_Nc6.key_decision: White should grab the center with d4

d4.idea: Occupy the center - the most principled
d4.why_good: Takes advantage of Black's unusual move order

nimzo_main.name: Nimzowitsch Main Line
nimzo_main.white_plan: Push e5 for space, develop Nf3-Be2-O-O, maintain the center
nimzo_main.black_plan: Challenge e5 with f6, develop Bf5 (before e6!), castle and counterattack

after_e5.key_decision: White has a space advantage with e5

Bf5.why_good: Active bishop, prepares f6 to challenge e5

e6.consequence: Black is cramped with no active piece play
e6.learning: Always develop bishops before playing e6 in closed positions

nimzo_nf3.name: Nimzowitsch vs Nf3
nimzo_nf3.white_plan: Develop with tempo against the queen, build a solid center
nimzo_nf3.black_plan: Transpose to Scandinavian-like positions, develop actively

Nc3.why_good: Standard - forces the queen to move again

common_learnings: The Nimzowitsch Defense is a surprise weapon - opponents won't know the theory
Nc6 on move 1 is unusual but not bad - it has hypermodern ideas
Black often transposes into other openings (Scandinavian, French) from this setup
Develop the light bishop before playing e6 - the same principle as Caro-Kann and Slav
Best suited for players who enjoy unusual positions and catching opponents off guard

four_knights.white_plan: Develop all four knights, control the center, play d4
four_knights.black_plan: Mirror development, keep the center balanced

traps.name: Halloween Gambit
traps.explanation: White gives up a knight for one pawn but gets a huge pawn center with d4-d5-e5. Black's pieces get pushed all the way back to the starting squares.
traps.refutation: After Nxe5, play Nc6 then Bb4 to pin the knight. Black keeps the extra piece.

traps.name: Englund Gambit Trap
traps.explanation: White thinks Bc3 traps the queen. But Bb4 pins the bishop to the king! After Bxb4 Qxa1, Black wins a rook.
traps.refutation: Do NOT play Bf4. Play Qd5, e3, or Nc3 instead.

albin_counter_gambit.white_plan: Accept the gambit, hold the center

traps.name: Lasker Trap
traps.explanation: The pawn promotes to a KNIGHT not a queen! The knight gives check and forks king and rook. One of the most beautiful underpromotions in chess.
traps.refutation: Do NOT play e3. Play Nf3 instead. If e3, after dxe3 play fxe3 not Bxb4.
